turn_text: Hello and welcome to Cammie's podcast. I'm your host, Congressman John Faso. I served as U.S. Representative for New York's 19th Congressional District from 2017 to 2019. That's located in the Hudson Valley and Catskill region of upstate New York. Cami is the center for accountability, modernization, and innovation. It's an organization dedicated to improving the delivery of government services to improve the customer experience throughout the country. That means serving citizens better. Cami believes that government programs and contracting must run efficiently and with integrity. The government must be responsive, transparent, and most of all a responsible steward of taxpayer dollars. That leads us to today's podcast topic. We're diving into the SNAP state of play. Now SNAP, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, used to be called food stamps. But for about the last 10 or 15 years, it's been called SNAP. It's a really important program that serves millions of American families. We'll review the situation across the country, focusing on some states as case studies show just how bad SNAP performance actually is and what are the possible solutions that we can employ to resolve these backlogs. What's the situation across the country? Well, According to our review of the state reporting and statistics filed with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, at least three in four states are now failing to meet the timeliness requirements for a SNAP application to be processed. That means that in at least 38 states, are failing to meet the federally required timeframes. And the time frame is a 30 days to process an application for most applicants, and a week, seven days for those that are in a family emergency. And this impacts millions of American families, more than 40 million, in fact, Americans are on food stamps. Earlier this year, 47 states and territories received letters from the U.S. Department of Agriculture on this issue. Thirty-five of those letters concerned their failures to meet those processing time requirements, and a number of states were even subject to financial penalties given their performances last year and in 2022. And we're talking primarily about Alaska, Oregon, Hawaii, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Delaware, and the District of Columbia. These penalties, by the way, can total millions of dollars. Now, just how bad is it? Well, states can't hire enough staff from public employee union rosters by their own admission. And the states are having the same kind of difficulty that private sector employers are having. They can't find people to work. For example, a news report out of why this month says that SNAP benefits are being delayed due to surge in applications and public staff vacancies. DHS says that nearly a quarter of positions for workers who process applications in Hawaii have not been filled. Hawaii reports that it receives three to 400 new applications for SNAP benefits every single day. And the situation in our northern neighbor up in Alaska is only getting worse. Alaskans are actually suing the state over food assistance delays and asking courts to order faster application processing, an attorney working on the case up there told Alaska Public Media that this is a very, very significant crisis and that they have not seen a crisis of this proportion in many years. Consider this, Alaska has been struggling with major delays since the winter of 2022. Perhaps that was a hangover from the COVID-19 pandemic. The state health commissioner designee recently received a five-page letter of reprimand from the USDA, and that was back in February of 23. But by the next month, there were still about 9,000 Alaskans whose SNAP applications from the year before had not still been processed. a reminder that it's supposed to take as long as a month to process, apparently fell on deaf ears with state officials. And I hate to blame the state officials, because frankly, they're having a really hard time filling the jobs for people to process these applications. People in Alaska were reporting at the time that they had, quote, dire impacts, unquote. To regain control of the situation, Alaskans who were seeking recertification of their benefits around that time, which was the late winter and early spring of 2023, had their benefits automatically renewed for six months, at the last time we checked less than half of the new applications were being processed on time in Alaska, even as there was an emphasis on trying to solve the crisis. And in the nation's capital in Washington, D.C., the District of Columbia faces a $4.4 million federal penalty for poor SNAP performance. Now, Pulitzer prize-winning columnist with The Washington Post, a fellow named Colbert King, who I've read for you many years, he wrote about his disgust that when stating that, quote, the USDA considers 6% to be an acceptable error rate in processing SNAP benefits, In 20% of the cases, USDA data shows DC overpaid or underpaid benefits to SNAP recipients." He detailed what happened at a recent District of Columbia council meeting when council members were confronted with this information and he wrote, will the council hold city leaders accountable? Or will it bluff and bluster and divter, letting them skate on and leaving families without food on the table? Cammie Chairman Stan Soloway in a response to King's op-ed in the post points out that this failure to administer DC's food aid system is not unique to the district. These kind of failures are increasingly plaguing states across the country. It's really unfortunate. What can be done to fix these backlogs and getting food on the table for struggling American families? And I would note that the backlogs and the USDA penalties, it's not a blue or red state kind of issue. It's states that are run by both Democrats and Republicans are having this problem. So it's a broad systemic problem in terms of how SNAP is administered. Now, states, what is a solution? I think states need to have flexibility to hire contractors to help them get over these backlogs, get over the hump of these backlogged applications. States can provide the flexibility to hire a temporary workforce without replacing current jobs or substituting the current jobs. to quickly adjudicate SNAP applications. States after all pay for 50% of the administrative costs to run the SNAP program, so states should have the option to run their program in the most efficient manner, including hiring contractors And that solution is contained in legislation that's actually been offered in Congress, a representative Don Bacon from Nebraska, who's a member of the Agriculture Committee. He pushed a snap flexibility proposal which would authorize states to hire contractors to let them get over backlogs that are brought about by public health emergencies like the pandemic that we recently went through, or if you have a natural disaster, a hurricane, an earthquake, tornadoes, where you have all of a sudden a large influx of applications coming in. The Bacon Bill would allow states to hire contractors on a temporary basis, bring them in to help solve the problem, and then when the problem goes away, then the state doesn't need to have the contractors. So I think that this is something. When I was in Congress, in fact, on the Agriculture Committee, I offered a similar proposal which was adopted by the House of Representatives in an amendment that I offered. Unfortunately, it didn't make it through the process in the last farm bill in 2018 because there was some opposition in the US Senate to it. But this is a common sense solution to a big problem that's affecting states all across the country. This has been a big issue in my state, in New York, in small rural upstate counties, as well as in the city of New York. This has been an issue. And the only viable solution, the only legislative solution that's been offered is the one that Congressman Bacon is suggesting. So I hope this has given you a little information about how SNAP benefits, which are critically important to families who are hungry and who might be suffering a job loss or a disability. It's a really critical government work better to deliver these services when people are eligible. The Bacon bill will expedite the process and it will provide states an option to bring on folks who can help them get over the backlog that they're trying to deal with in the snap space. So in conclusion, we're going to find out in the next couple of months because the Farm Bill is expiring in September. We're going to find out in the next few months whether or not the Congress actually acts to address this significant problem. Again, 47 states and territories have been sanctioned or admonished by the U.S. Department of Agriculture because they're not processing applications on time, it's not fair and it's unacceptable that hungry Americans are being forced to wait months, potentially up to a year to have their SNAP applications process. Now, for more information about this issue and more information about Cammy, as well as the State of Play on Snap, you can visit our website, thecenterforami.org, thecenterforami.org. This is Congressman John Faso and thanks for listening.
